title: Book 4, Chapter 12 — Seventh Year of the War—Occupation of Pylos—Surrender of the Spartan Army in Sphacteria
paragraphs: Next summer, about the time the corn was coming into ear, ten Syracusan and as many Locrian vessels sailed to Messina, in Sicily, and occupied the town at the invitation of the inhabitants; and Messina revolted from the Athenians. The Syracusans contrived this chiefly because they saw the place gave them an approach to Sicily and feared that the Athenians might later use it as a base for attacking them with a larger force. The Locrians did so because they wished to carry on hostilities from both sides of the strait and reduce their enemies, the people of Rhegium. Meanwhile the Locrians had invaded Rhegian territory with all their forces, to prevent them helping Messina, and also at the urging of some Rhegian exiles who were with them; the long factional struggles by which Rhegium had been torn made it for the moment incapable of resistance, and so provided an additional temptation for the invaders. After devastating the country the Locrian land forces withdrew, their ships remaining to guard Messina, while others were being manned for the same destination to carry on the war from there.

About the same time in the spring, before the corn was ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under Agis, son of Archidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and sat down and laid waste the country. Meanwhile the Athenians sent off the forty ships they had been preparing for Sicily, with the remaining generals Eurymedon and Sophocles; their colleague Pythodorus had already gone ahead. These had also been instructed to look in, as they sailed by, on the Corcyraeans in the town, who were being plundered by the exiles in the mountains. To support these exiles, sixty Peloponnesian vessels had recently sailed there, since it was thought that the famine raging in the city would make it easy for them to reduce it. Demosthenes too, who had remained without employment since his return from Acarnania, applied for and obtained permission to use the fleet, if he wished, on the coast of the Peloponnese.

Off Laconia they heard that the Peloponnesian ships were already at Corcyra, and Eurymedon and Sophocles wished to hurry to the island. But Demosthenes asked them first to touch at Pylos and do what was needed there before continuing the voyage. While they were objecting, a squall came on and carried the fleet into Pylos. Demosthenes at once urged them to fortify the place—it was for this that he had come on the voyage—and pointed out that there was plenty of stone and timber on the spot, that the place was strong by nature, and that, together with much of the country round, it was unoccupied. Pylos, or Coryphasium, as the Lacedaemonians call it, is about forty-five miles from Sparta, and lies in the old country of the Messenians. The commanders told him that there was no shortage of deserted headlands in the Peloponnese if he wanted to put the city to expense by occupying them. He thought, however, that this place was distinguished from others of its kind by having a harbour close by, and that the Messenians, the old natives of the country, who spoke the same dialect as the Lacedaemonians, could do them the greatest harm by raids from it, and would at the same time make a trustworthy garrison.

After speaking to the captains of companies on the subject and failing to persuade either the generals or the soldiers, he stayed inactive with the rest because of the weather; until the soldiers themselves, wanting something to do, were seized with a sudden impulse to go round and fortify the place. They set to work in earnest. Having no iron tools, they picked up stones and put them together as they happened to fit; and where mortar was needed, they carried it on their backs for want of hods, stooping down to keep it on, and clasping their hands together behind to prevent it falling off. They spared no effort to be able to complete the most vulnerable points before the Lacedaemonians arrived, since most of the place was sufficiently strong by nature to need no further fortification.

Meanwhile the Lacedaemonians were celebrating a festival, and at first they made light of the news, thinking that whenever they chose to take the field the place would be immediately abandoned by the enemy or easily taken by force; the absence of their army before Athens also had something to do with their delay. The Athenians fortified the place on the land side, and where it most required it, in six days, and leaving Demosthenes with five ships to garrison it, hurried on with the main body of the fleet on their voyage to Corcyra and Sicily.

As soon as the Peloponnesians in Attica heard of the occupation of Pylos, they hurried back home; the Lacedaemonians and their king Agis felt that the matter touched them closely. Besides having made their invasion early in the season, while the corn was still green, most of their troops were short of provisions; the weather too was unusually bad for the time of year, and greatly distressed their army. Many reasons combined to hasten their departure and make this invasion a very short one—indeed they only stayed fifteen days in Attica.

About the same time the Athenian general Simonides, gathering a few Athenians from the garrisons and a number of allies in those parts, took Eion in Thrace, a Mendaean colony hostile to Athens, by treachery. But no sooner had he done so than the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans came up and beat him out of it, with the loss of many of his soldiers.

On the return of the Peloponnesians from Attica, the Spartans themselves and the nearest of the Perioeci at once set out for Pylos, the other Lacedaemonians following more slowly, since they had just come in from another campaign. Word was also sent round the Peloponnese to come up as quickly as possible to Pylos. The sixty Peloponnesian ships were summoned from Corcyra, and being dragged by their crews across the isthmus of Leucas, passed unnoticed by the Athenian squadron at Zacynthus and reached Pylos, where the land forces had arrived before them. Before the Peloponnesian fleet sailed in, Demosthenes found time to send out, unobserved, two ships to inform Eurymedon and the Athenians on board the fleet at Zacynthus of the danger to Pylos and to summon them to his assistance. While the ships hastened on their voyage in obedience to Demosthenes’ orders, the Lacedaemonians prepared to assault the fort by land and sea, hoping easily to capture a work built in haste and held by a feeble garrison. Meanwhile, expecting the Athenian ships to arrive from Zacynthus, they intended, if they failed to take the place first, to block the entrances to the harbour to keep them from anchoring inside it. The island of Sphacteria, stretching in a line close in front of the harbour, both makes the harbour safe and narrows its entrances, leaving a passage for two ships on the side nearest Pylos and the Athenian fortifications, and for eight or nine on the side nearest the rest of the mainland. The rest of the island was entirely covered with wood and trackless, since uninhabited, and about one mile and five furlongs in length. The Lacedaemonians meant to close the inlets with a line of ships placed close together, prows turned toward the sea. Meanwhile, fearing that the enemy might use the island as a base against them, they carried over some heavy infantry to it, stationing others along the coast. By this means the island and the mainland would both be hostile to the Athenians, who would not be able to land on either; and the shore of Pylos itself, outside the inlet toward the open sea, having no harbour, offered no point that could be used as a base to relieve their countrymen. Without a sea-fight or risk, the Lacedaemonians would in all likelihood become masters of a place taken on the spur of the moment and unprovided with provisions. With this decided, they carried over to the island the heavy infantry, drafted by lot from all the companies. Some others had crossed earlier in relief parties, but those who were left there in this final draft numbered four hundred and twenty, with their Helot attendants, commanded by Epitadas, son of Molobrus.

Meanwhile Demosthenes, seeing that the Lacedaemonians were about to attack him by sea and land at once, was not idle. He drew up under the fortification, and enclosed in a stockade, the galleys remaining to him from those left him, arming the sailors taken out of them with poor shields, most of them made of osier; for it was impossible to procure arms in such a deserted place, and even these had been obtained from a thirty-oared Messenian privateer and a boat belonging to some Messenians who happened to have come there. Among these Messenians were forty heavy infantry, whom he made use of with the rest. He posted most of his men, armed and unarmed, on the best-fortified and strongest points of the place toward the interior, with orders to repel any attack of the land forces. He picked sixty heavy infantry and a few archers from his whole force, and with these went outside the wall down to the sea, where he thought the enemy would most likely try to land. The ground was difficult and rocky, looking out toward the open sea; but the very fact that this was the weakest part of the wall would, he thought, encourage their eagerness, since the Athenians, confident in their naval superiority, had paid little attention to the defences here, and the enemy, if he could force a landing, might feel sure of taking the place. At this point, accordingly, going down to the water’s edge, he posted his heavy infantry to prevent a landing if possible, and encouraged them with these words:

“Soldiers and comrades in this adventure, I hope none of you in our present strait will think to show his wit by exactly calculating all the perils that surround us. I hope rather that you will hasten to close with the enemy without staying to count the odds, seeing in this our best chance of safety. In emergencies like ours, calculation is out of place; the sooner the danger is faced, the better. To my mind, too, most of the chances are for us, if we will only stand fast and not throw away our advantages, overawed by the enemy’s numbers. One point in our favour is the awkwardness of the landing. This, however, only helps us if we stand our ground. If we give way it will be practicable enough, in spite of its natural difficulty, with no defender; and the enemy will at once become more formidable, since retreat will be hard for him if we manage to repulse him—which we shall find easier to do while he is on board his ships than after he has landed and meets us on equal terms. As to his numbers, do not be too alarmed. Large as they are, he can only engage in small detachments, since it is impossible for many to put in to shore at once. Besides, the numerical superiority we have to face is not that of an army on land with everything else equal, but of troops on board ship, where many favourable accidents are needed to bring numbers to bear. I therefore consider that his difficulties may fairly be set against our numerical inferiority. At the same time, I charge you, as Athenians who know by experience what landing from ships on hostile territory means, and how impossible it is to drive back an enemy determined enough to stand his ground and not to be frightened off by the surf or the terrors of incoming ships, to stand fast in this present emergency, beat the enemy back at the water’s edge, and save yourselves and the place.”

Thus encouraged by Demosthenes, the Athenians felt more confident, and went down to meet the enemy, posting themselves along the edge of the sea. The Lacedaemonians now moved forward and at the same time assaulted the fortification with their land forces and their ships—forty-three in number—under their admiral, Thrasymelidas, son of Cratesicles, a Spartan, who made his attack just where Demosthenes expected. The Athenians thus had to defend themselves on both sides, from land and from sea. The enemy rowed up in small detachments, one relieving the other—it being impossible for many to put in at once—showing great ardour and cheering each other on, in the effort to force a passage and take the fortification. The man who most distinguished himself was Brasidas. Captain of a galley, and seeing that the captains and steersmen, struck by the difficulty of the position, hung back even where a landing seemed possible, for fear of wrecking their vessels, he shouted to them that they must never allow the enemy to fortify himself in their country for the sake of saving timber, but must shatter their ships and force a landing. He told the allies, instead of hesitating at such a moment to sacrifice their ships for Lacedaemon in return for her many benefits, to run them boldly aground, land in one way or another, and make themselves masters of the place and its garrison.

Not content with this exhortation, he forced his own steersman to run his ship ashore, and stepping onto the gangway was attempting to land when he was cut down by the Athenians, and after receiving many wounds fainted away. Falling into the bows, his shield slipped off his arm into the sea, was washed ashore, and was picked up by the Athenians, who afterwards used it for the trophy they set up for this attack. The rest also did their best, but were unable to land, owing to the difficulty of the ground and the unflinching tenacity of the Athenians. It was a strange reversal of the order of things for Athenians to be fighting from the land—and from Laconian land too—against Lacedaemonians coming from the sea, while the Lacedaemonians were trying to land from shipboard in their own country, now turned hostile, in order to attack Athenians; though the former were chiefly famous at the time as an inland people superior on land, and the latter as a maritime people with a navy that had no equal.

After continuing their attacks during that day and most of the next, the Peloponnesians desisted, and the day after sent some of their ships to Asine for timber to make engines, hoping with their help to take, in spite of its height, the wall opposite the harbour, where the landing was easiest. At this moment the Athenian fleet from Zacynthus arrived, now numbering fifty sail, having been reinforced by some of the ships on guard at Naupactus and by four Chian vessels. Seeing the coast and the island both crowded with heavy infantry, and the hostile ships in harbour showing no signs of sailing out, at a loss where to anchor, they sailed for the moment to the deserted island of Prote, not far off, where they spent the night. The next day they got under way, ready to engage in the open sea if the enemy chose to come out and meet them, and determined, if he did not, to sail in and attack him. The Lacedaemonians did not put out, and having failed to close the inlets as they had intended, remained quiet on shore, busy manning their ships and getting ready, in case anyone sailed in, to fight inside the harbour, which is fairly large.

Seeing this, the Athenians advanced against them by each inlet, and falling on the enemy’s fleet, most of which by this time was afloat and in line, at once put it to flight. Giving chase as far as the short distance allowed, they disabled a good many vessels and took five, one with its crew on board. They dashed in at the rest that had taken refuge on shore, battered some that were still being manned before they could put out, lashed others to their own ships and towed them off empty after the crews had fled. At this sight the Lacedaemonians, maddened by a disaster which cut off their men on the island, rushed to the rescue, going into the sea in their heavy armour, laying hold of the ships and trying to drag them back, every man thinking that success depended on his own exertions. Great was the melee, and quite contrary to the naval tactics usual to the two combatants: the Lacedaemonians in their excitement and dismay were actually engaged in a sea-fight on land, while the victorious Athenians, eager to push their success as far as possible, were carrying on a land-fight from their ships. After great exertions and many wounds on both sides, they separated, the Lacedaemonians saving their empty ships, except those first taken; and both parties returning to their camp, the Athenians set up a trophy, gave back the dead, secured the wrecks, and at once began to cruise round and watch the island jealously, with its trapped garrison; while the Peloponnesians on the mainland, whose contingents had now all come up, stayed where they were before Pylos.

When the news of what had happened at Pylos reached Sparta, the disaster was thought so serious that the Lacedaemonians resolved that the authorities should go down to the camp and decide on the spot what was best to be done. There, seeing it was impossible to help their men, and not wishing to risk their being reduced by hunger or overpowered by numbers, they determined, with the consent of the Athenian generals, to conclude an armistice at Pylos and send envoys to Athens to obtain a settlement and try to recover their men as quickly as possible.
The generals accepted their offers, and an armistice was concluded on the following terms:

That the Lacedaemonians should bring to Pylos and hand over to the Athenians the ships that had fought in the recent engagement, and all the warships in Laconia, and should make no attack on the fortification either by land or by sea.

That the Athenians should allow the Lacedaemonians on the mainland to send to the men on the island a fixed quantity of corn ready kneaded—two quarts of barley meal, one pint of wine, and a piece of meat for each man, and half the same quantity for a servant.
That this allowance should be sent in under the eyes of the Athenians, and that no boat should sail to the island except openly.
That the Athenians should continue to watch the island as before, but not land on it, and should refrain from attacking the Peloponnesian troops either by land or by sea.
That if either party should infringe any of these terms in the slightest particular, the armistice should at once be void.

That the armistice should hold until the return of the Lacedaemonian envoys from Athens—the Athenians sending them there in a galley and bringing them back—and on the arrival of the envoys should end, and the ships be restored by the Athenians in the same state as they received them.
Such were the terms of the armistice, and the ships were handed over to the number of sixty, and the envoys sent off accordingly. On reaching Athens they spoke as follows:

“Athenians, the Lacedaemonians have sent us to try to find some way of settling the affair of our men on the island, in a manner at once satisfactory to our interests and as consistent with our dignity in misfortune as circumstances permit. We can venture to speak at some length, without departing from the habit of our country. Men of few words where many are not wanted, we can be less brief when there is a matter of importance to be illustrated, and an end to be served by its illustration. Meanwhile we beg you to take what we say not in a hostile spirit, nor as if we thought you ignorant and wished to lecture you, but rather as a suggestion on the best course to be taken, addressed to intelligent judges. You can now, if you choose, employ your present success to advantage—keep what you have got and gain honour and reputation besides—and you can avoid the mistake of those who meet with an extraordinary piece of good fortune and are led on by hope to grasp continually at something further, having already succeeded beyond their expectations. Those who have known the most ups and downs of fortune are also rightly the least disposed to trust their prosperity; and to teach your city and ours this lesson, experience has not been wanting.

“To be convinced of this, you have only to look at our present misfortune. What power in Hellas stood higher than ours? Yet here we are coming to you, although we used to think ourselves more able to grant what we are now here to ask. Nevertheless, we have not been brought to this by any decay in our power, or by having had our heads turned by aggrandisement; our resources are what they have always been, and our error has been an error of judgment, to which all are equally liable. The prosperity that your city now enjoys, and the additions it has lately received, must not therefore make you fancy that fortune will always be with you. Sensible men are prudent enough to treat their gains as precarious, just as they would also keep a clear head in adversity, and they think that war, far from staying within the limits a combatant may wish to confine it to, will run the course its chances prescribe. Thus, not being puffed up by confidence in military success, they are less likely to come to grief, and most ready to make peace, if they can, while their fortune lasts. This, Athenians, is a good opportunity for you to do now with us, and so to escape the possible disasters that may follow from refusal—and the consequent imputation of having owed even your present advantages to accident, when you might have left behind you a reputation for power and wisdom that nothing could endanger.

“The Lacedaemonians accordingly invite you to make a treaty and to end the war, and offer peace, alliance, and the most friendly and intimate relations in every way and on every occasion between us; and in return ask for the men on the island, thinking it better for both parties not to hold out to the end—on the chance of some favourable accident enabling the men to force their way out, or of their being compelled to succumb under the pressure of blockade. Indeed, if great enmities are ever to be really settled, we think it will not be by the system of revenge and military success, by forcing an opponent to swear to a treaty to his disadvantage; but when the more fortunate combatant waives these privileges, lets gentler feelings guide him, conquers his rival in generosity, and grants peace on more moderate conditions than expected. From that moment, instead of the debt of revenge that violence must entail, his adversary owes a debt of generosity to be repaid in kind, and is inclined by honour to stand by his agreement. Men more often act in this way toward their greatest enemies than where the quarrel is of less importance; they are also by nature as glad to give way to those who first yield to them as they are quick to be provoked by arrogance into risks their own judgment condemns.

“To apply this to ourselves: if peace was ever desirable for both parties, it is surely so at the present moment—before anything irremediable happens to us and forces us to hate you eternally, personally as well as politically, and you to miss the advantages we now offer you. While the issue is still in doubt, and you have reputation and our friendship in prospect, and we the compromise of our misfortune before anything fatal has occurred, let us be reconciled. Choose peace instead of war for ourselves, and grant the rest of the Hellenes a remission from their sufferings, for which, you may be sure, they will think they have chiefly you to thank. The war that they are suffering through, they do not know which side started; but the peace that ends it, since it depends on your decision, will be laid to your door by their gratitude. By such a decision you can become firm friends with the Lacedaemonians at their own invitation—not forced from them, but obliged by your acceptance. Consider too the advantages likely to follow from this friendship: when Attica and Sparta are at one, the rest of Hellas, you may be sure, will remain in respectful inferiority before its leaders.”

Such were the words of the Lacedaemonians. Their idea was that the Athenians, already wanting a truce and held back only by their opposition, would joyfully accept a peace freely offered and give back the men. The Athenians, however, having the men on the island, thought that the treaty would be ready for them whenever they chose to make it, and grasped at something further. Foremost in encouraging them in this policy was Cleon, son of Cleaenetus, a popular leader of the time, very powerful with the multitude, who persuaded them to answer as follows. First, the men on the island must surrender themselves and their arms and be brought to Athens. Next, the Lacedaemonians must restore Nisaea, Pegae, Troezen, and Achaia—all places acquired not by arms but by the previous convention, under which they had been ceded by Athens herself at a moment of disaster, when a truce was more necessary to her than at present. This done, they could take their men back and make a truce for as long as both parties might agree.

To this answer the envoys made no reply, but asked that commissioners be chosen with whom they might confer on each point, quietly talking the matter over and trying to come to some agreement. At this Cleon violently attacked them, saying he had known from the first they had no honest intentions, and that this was now plain enough from their refusing to speak before the people and wanting instead to confer in secret with a committee of two or three. If they meant anything honest, let them say it out before all. The Lacedaemonians, however, seeing that whatever concessions they might be prepared to make in their misfortune, it was impossible to speak before the multitude and lose credit with their allies for a negotiation that might in the end miscarry, and on the other hand that the Athenians would never grant what they asked on moderate terms, returned from Athens having achieved nothing.

Their arrival at once put an end to the armistice at Pylos, and the Lacedaemonians asked back their ships under the convention. The Athenians, however, alleged an attack on the fort in violation of the truce, along with other grievances seemingly not worth mentioning, and refused to give them back, insisting on the clause by which the slightest infringement made the armistice void. The Lacedaemonians, after denying the violation and protesting against bad faith in the matter of the ships, went away and earnestly addressed themselves to the war. Hostilities were now carried on at Pylos with vigour on both sides. The Athenians cruised round the island all day with two ships going opposite ways, and at night anchored round it with their whole fleet, except on the seaward side in windy weather. The fleet had been reinforced by twenty ships from Athens come to aid in the blockade, and now numbered seventy sail. The Peloponnesians remained encamped on the continent, making attacks on the fort and watching for any opportunity that might offer for the deliverance of their men.

Meanwhile the Syracusans and their allies in Sicily had brought up to the squadron guarding Messina the reinforcement we left them preparing, and were carrying on the war from there, incited chiefly by the Locrians out of hatred for the Rhegians, whose territory they had invaded with all their forces. The Syracusans also wished to try their fortune at sea, seeing that the Athenians had only a few ships actually at Rhegium, and hearing that the main fleet meant to join them was engaged in blockading the island. A naval victory, they thought, would let them blockade Rhegium by sea and land and easily reduce it; a success that would at once place their affairs on a solid footing, since the promontory of Rhegium in Italy and Messina in Sicily are so near each other that it would be impossible for the Athenians to cruise against them and command the strait. The strait in question consists of the sea between Rhegium and Messina, at the point where Sicily comes nearest to the continent, and is the Charybdis through which the story makes Ulysses sail. The narrowness of the passage and the strength of the current that pours in from the vast Tyrrhenian and Sicilian mains have rightly given it a bad reputation.

In this strait the Syracusans and their allies were forced to fight, late in the day, over the passage of a boat, putting out with rather more than thirty ships against sixteen Athenian and eight Rhegian vessels. Defeated by the Athenians, they hurried off, each man for himself, to their own stations at Messina and Rhegium, with the loss of one ship; night came on before the battle was finished. After this the Locrians retired from Rhegian territory, and the ships of the Syracusans and their allies united and came to anchor at Cape Pelorus, in Messinian territory, where their land forces joined them. Here the Athenians and Rhegians sailed up, and seeing the ships unmanned, made an attack, in which they in turn lost one vessel, caught by a grappling iron, the crew saving themselves by swimming. After this the Syracusans got on board their ships, and while they were being towed alongshore to Messina were attacked again by the Athenians, but suddenly got out to sea and became the assailants, causing them to lose another vessel. After thus holding their own in the voyage alongshore and in the engagement just described, the Syracusans sailed on into the harbour of Messina.

Meanwhile the Athenians, having received warning that Camarina was about to be betrayed to the Syracusans by Archias and his party, sailed there. The Messinese took this opportunity to attack their Chalcidian neighbour, Naxos, by sea and land with all their forces. The first day they forced the Naxians to keep within their walls, and laid waste their country; the next they sailed round with their ships and laid waste their land along the river Akesines, while their land forces threatened the city. Meanwhile the Sicels came down from the high country in great numbers, to aid against the Messinese; and the Naxians, elated at the sight, and animated by a belief that the Leontines and their other Hellenic allies were coming to support them, suddenly sallied out from the town, attacked, and routed the Messinese, killing more than a thousand of them. The remainder suffered severely on their retreat home, attacked by the barbarians on the road, and most of them were cut off. The ships put in at Messina, and afterwards dispersed for their various homes. The Leontines and their allies, with the Athenians, at once turned their arms against the now weakened Messina, and attacked—the Athenians with their ships on the side of the harbour, the land forces on the side of the town. The Messinese, however, sallying out with Demoteles and some Locrians who had been left to garrison the city after the disaster, suddenly attacked and routed most of the Leontine army, killing a great number. On seeing this the Athenians landed from their ships, and falling on the Messinese in disorder chased them back into the town, and after setting up a trophy retired to Rhegium. After this the Hellenes in Sicily continued to make war on each other by land, without the Athenians.

Meanwhile the Athenians at Pylos were still besieging the Lacedaemonians on the island, the Peloponnesian forces on the mainland remaining where they were. The blockade was very laborious for the Athenians from want of food and water; there was no spring except one in the citadel of Pylos itself, and that not a large one, and most of them were forced to grub up the shingle on the sea beach and drink such water as they could find. They also suffered from lack of room, being encamped in a narrow space; and as there was no anchorage for the ships, some took their meals on shore in turn while the others were anchored out at sea. But their greatest discouragement came from the unexpectedly long time it was taking to reduce a body of men shut up on a deserted island, with only brackish water to drink—a matter they had imagined would take only a few days. The fact was that the Lacedaemonians had advertised for volunteers to carry into the island ground corn, wine, cheese, and any other food useful in a siege; high prices were offered, and freedom promised to any of the Helots who succeeded in doing so. The Helots accordingly were most forward to engage in this risky traffic, putting off from this or that part of the Peloponnese and running in by night on the seaward side of the island. They were best pleased, however, when they could catch a wind to carry them in. It was easier to evade the patrol of galleys when it blew from the seaward, since it became impossible for them to anchor round the island; and the Helots, having had their boats valued in money, ran them ashore without caring how they landed, sure of finding the soldiers waiting at the landing places. But all who risked it in fair weather were taken. Divers also swam in under water from the harbour, dragging by a cord in skins poppyseed mixed with honey, and bruised linseed; these at first escaped notice, but afterwards a watch was kept for them. In short, both sides tried every possible contrivance, the one to throw in provisions, the other to prevent their introduction.

At Athens, meanwhile, the news that the army was in great distress, and that corn was finding its way in to the men on the island, caused no small perplexity. The Athenians began to fear that winter might come on and find them still engaged in the blockade. They saw that convoying provisions round the Peloponnese would then be impossible. The country offered no resources in itself, and even in summer they could not send round enough. The blockade of a place without harbours could no longer be kept up; and the men would either escape, by the siege being abandoned, or watch for bad weather and sail out in the boats that brought their corn. What caused still more alarm was the attitude of the Lacedaemonians, who, the Athenians thought, must feel themselves on strong ground not to send any more envoys; and they began to repent having rejected the treaty. Cleon, perceiving the disfavour with which he was regarded for having stood in the way of the convention, now said that the informants did not speak the truth; and when the messengers recommended that, if they did not believe them, some commissioners be sent to see, Cleon himself and Theagenes were chosen by the Athenians as commissioners. Aware that he would now be obliged either to say what had already been said by the men he was slandering, or be proved a liar if he said the contrary, he told the Athenians—whom he saw were not entirely disinclined for a fresh expedition—that, instead of sending and wasting their time and opportunities, if they believed what they were told, they ought to sail against the men. And pointing at Nicias, son of Niceratus, then general, whom he hated, he tauntingly said that it would be easy, if they had men for generals, to sail with a force and take those on the island; and if he himself had been in command, he would have done it.

Nicias, seeing the Athenians murmuring against Cleon for not sailing now if it seemed to him so easy, and further seeing himself the object of attack, told him that for all the generals cared he might take what force he chose and make the attempt. At first Cleon thought this resignation was merely a figure of speech, and was ready to go; but finding it was meant seriously he drew back, and said that Nicias, not he, was general, being now frightened, and never having supposed that Nicias would go so far as to retire in his favour. Nicias, however, repeated his offer, resigned the command against Pylos, and called the Athenians to witness that he did so. And as the multitude is wont to do, the more Cleon shrank from the expedition and tried to back out of what he had said, the more they encouraged Nicias to hand over his command, and clamoured for Cleon to go. At last, not knowing how to escape his words, he undertook the expedition, came forward, and said that he was not afraid of the Lacedaemonians, but would sail without taking anyone from the city with him, except the Lemnians and Imbrians who were at Athens, with some targeteers who had come up from Aenus, and four hundred archers from other quarters. With these and the soldiers at Pylos, he would within twenty days either bring the Lacedaemonians back alive or kill them on the spot. The Athenians could not help laughing at his fatuity, while sensible men comforted themselves with the reflection that they were bound to gain in either case: either they would be rid of Cleon, which they rather hoped, or, if disappointed in this hope, they would reduce the Lacedaemonians.

After he had settled everything in the assembly, and the Athenians had voted him the command of the expedition, he chose as his colleague Demosthenes, one of the generals at Pylos, and pushed forward preparations for the voyage. His choice fell on Demosthenes because he heard that he was contemplating a descent on the island. The soldiers, distressed by the difficulties of the position, and rather besieged than besiegers, were eager to fight it out, while the firing of the island had increased their general’s confidence. He had been afraid at first because the island, never having been inhabited, was almost entirely covered with wood and trackless, thinking this in the enemy’s favour: he might land with a large force and yet suffer loss from an attack from an unseen position. The enemy’s mistakes and the strength of his forces would be largely concealed from him by the wood, while every blunder of his own troops would be at once detected, so that they could fall on him unexpectedly just where they pleased, the attack being always in their power. If, on the other hand, he forced them to engage in the thicket, the smaller number who knew the country would, he thought, have the advantage over the larger who did not, while his own army might be cut off imperceptibly, despite its numbers, since the men would not be able to see where to help one another.

The Aetolian disaster, which had been mainly caused by the wood, had no small part in these reflections. Meanwhile, one of the soldiers who were forced by want of room to land on the extremities of the island and take their dinners, with outposts set to prevent surprise, set fire to a little of the wood without meaning to; and as it came on to blow soon afterwards, almost the whole was consumed before they realised what had happened. Demosthenes was now able for the first time to see how numerous the Lacedaemonians really were—up to that moment he had been under the impression that they took in provisions for a smaller number. He also saw that the Athenians thought success important and were anxious about it, and that it was now easier to land on the island. Accordingly he got ready for the attempt, sent for troops from the allies in the neighbourhood, and pushed forward his other preparations. At this moment Cleon arrived at Pylos with the troops he had asked for, having sent word ahead that he was coming. The first step taken by the two generals after meeting was to send a herald to the camp on the mainland, to ask if they were disposed to avoid all risk and order the men on the island to surrender themselves and their arms, to be kept in mild custody until some general convention should be concluded.

On the rejection of this proposal, the generals let one day pass; the next, embarking all their heavy infantry on a few ships, they put out by night, and a little before dawn landed on both sides of the island from the open sea and from the harbour, about eight hundred strong, and advanced at a run against the first post on the island.

The enemy had distributed his force as follows. At this first post there were about thirty heavy infantry; the centre and most level part, where the water was, was held by the main body and by Epitadas their commander; while a small party guarded the very end of the island, toward Pylos, which was sheer on the seaward side and very hard to attack from the land, and where there was also a sort of old fort of stones rudely put together, which they thought might be useful to them if they were forced to retreat. Such was their disposition.

The advanced post thus attacked by the Athenians was at once put to the sword, the men being scarcely out of bed and still arming, the landing having taken them by surprise, since they thought the ships were only sailing as usual to their stations for the night. As soon as day broke, the rest of the army landed—that is, all the crews of rather more than seventy ships, except the lowest rank of oars, with the arms they carried, eight hundred archers, and as many targeteers, the Messenian reinforcements, and all the other troops on duty round Pylos, except the garrison on the fort. Demosthenes’ tactics had divided them into companies of two hundred, more or less, and sent them to occupy the highest points, in order to paralyse the enemy by surrounding him on every side and so leaving him without any tangible adversary, exposed to the cross-fire of their host. He would be plied by those in his rear if he attacked in front, and by those on one flank if he moved against those on the other. In short, wherever he went he would have the assailants behind him; and these light-armed assailants were the most awkward of all—their arrows, darts, stones, and slings making them formidable at a distance, with no way of getting at them at close quarters, since they could conquer in flight, and the moment their pursuer turned they were upon him. Such was the idea that inspired Demosthenes in his conception of the descent, and that presided over its execution.

Meanwhile the main body of the troops on the island (those under Epitadas), seeing their outpost cut off and an army advancing against them, closed ranks and pressed forward to engage the Athenian heavy infantry in front of them, the light troops being on their flanks and rear. They were unable, however, either to engage or to make use of their superior skill, since the light troops kept them in check on either side with their missiles, and the heavy infantry remained stationary instead of advancing to meet them. Although they routed the light troops wherever they ran up and approached too closely, they retreated fighting, being lightly equipped and easily getting the start in flight, given the difficult and rugged ground of an island that had until then been deserted, over which the Lacedaemonians could not pursue them in their heavy armour.

After this skirmishing had gone on for a little while, the Lacedaemonians became unable to dash out with the same speed as before at the points attacked, and the light troops, seeing that they now fought with less vigour, became more confident. They could see with their own eyes that they were many times more numerous than the enemy; they were now more familiar with his look, and found him less terrible, since the result had not justified the apprehensions they had felt when they first landed in slavish dismay at the idea of attacking Lacedaemonians. Their fear changing to disdain, they now rushed all together with loud shouts upon them, pelting them with stones, darts, and arrows—whatever came first to hand. The shouting accompanying their onset confounded the Lacedaemonians, who were unaccustomed to this style of fighting; dust rose from the newly burnt wood, and it was impossible to see in front of one with the arrows and stones flying through clouds of dust from the hands of numerous assailants. The Lacedaemonians had now to endure a rude conflict; their caps would not keep out the arrows; darts had broken off in the armour of the wounded; while they themselves were helpless for offence, prevented from using their eyes to see what was in front of them, and unable to hear the words of command for the hubbub raised by the enemy. Danger encompassed them on every side, and there was no hope of any means of defence or safety.

At last, after many had already been wounded in the confined space in which they were fighting, they formed up in close order and retired on the fort at the end of the island, which was not far off, and to their friends who held it. The moment they gave way, the light troops became bolder and pressed on them, shouting louder than ever, and killing as many as they came up with in their retreat. Most of the Lacedaemonians, however, made good their escape to the fort, and with the garrison there ranged themselves all along its whole extent to repulse the enemy wherever it could be assailed. The Athenians, in pursuit, unable to surround and hem them in because of the strength of the ground, attacked them in front and tried to storm the position. For a long time, indeed for most of the day, both sides held out against all the torments of the battle, thirst, and sun, the one trying to drive the enemy from the high ground, the other to maintain himself on it. It was now easier for the Lacedaemonians to defend themselves than before, since they could no longer be surrounded on the flanks.

The struggle began to seem endless, when the commander of the Messenians came to Cleon and Demosthenes and told them they were wasting their efforts; but if they would give him some archers and light troops to go round to the enemy’s rear by a way he would undertake to find, he thought he could force the approach. On receiving what he asked for, he started from a point out of sight to avoid being seen by the enemy, and creeping on wherever the precipices of the island allowed, and where the Lacedaemonians, trusting to the strength of the ground, kept no guard, succeeded after the greatest difficulty in getting round without being seen, and suddenly appeared on the high ground in their rear, to the dismay of the surprised enemy and the still greater joy of his expectant friends. The Lacedaemonians, thus placed between two fires, in the same dilemma—to compare small things with great—as at Thermopylae, where the defenders were cut off through the Persians getting round by the path, being now attacked in front and behind, began to give way. Overcome by the odds against them and exhausted from want of food, they retreated.

The Athenians were already masters of the approaches when Cleon and Demosthenes, perceiving that if the enemy gave way a single step further they would be destroyed by their soldiery, put a stop to the battle and held their men back. They wished to take the Lacedaemonians alive to Athens, hoping that their stubbornness might relax on hearing the offer of terms, and that they might surrender and yield to the present overwhelming danger. Proclamation was accordingly made to ask if they would surrender themselves and their arms to the Athenians, to be dealt with at their discretion.

Hearing this offer, most of the Lacedaemonians lowered their shields and waved their hands to show that they accepted it. Hostilities now ceased, and a parley was held between Cleon and Demosthenes on one side, and Styphon, son of Pharax, on the other; for Epitadas, the first of the previous commanders, had been killed, and Hippagretas, the next in command, left for dead among the slain (though still alive), and so the command had devolved on Styphon according to the law, in case anything happened to his superiors. Styphon and his companions said they wished to send a herald to the Lacedaemonians on the mainland, to know what they were to do. The Athenians would not let any of them go, but themselves called for heralds from the mainland, and after questions had been carried back and forth two or three times, the last man to come over from the Lacedaemonians on the continent brought this message: “The Lacedaemonians bid you decide for yourselves, so long as you do nothing dishonourable.” On this, after consulting together, they surrendered themselves and their arms. The Athenians, after guarding them that day and night, the next morning set up a trophy on the island and got ready to sail, handing their prisoners in batches to be guarded by the captains of the galleys; and the Lacedaemonians sent a herald and took up their dead. The number of the killed and prisoners taken on the island was as follows: four hundred and twenty heavy infantry had crossed over; three hundred all but eight were taken alive to Athens; the rest were killed. About a hundred and twenty of the prisoners were Spartans. The Athenian loss was small, since the battle had not been fought at close quarters.

The blockade altogether, counting from the sea-fight to the battle on the island, had lasted seventy-two days. For twenty of these, during the absence of the envoys sent to negotiate peace, the men had provisions given to them; for the rest they were fed by the smugglers. Corn and other food were found on the island; the commander Epitadas had kept the men on half rations. The Athenians and Peloponnesians now each withdrew their forces from Pylos and went home; and crazy as Cleon’s promise was, he fulfilled it by bringing the men to Athens within the twenty days as he had pledged.

Nothing that happened in the war surprised the Hellenes so much as this. The opinion was that no force or famine could make the Lacedaemonians give up their arms, but that they would fight on as best they could and die with their weapons in their hands. Indeed people could scarcely believe that those who had surrendered were of the same stuff as the fallen. An Athenian ally, who some time later insultingly asked one of the prisoners from the island whether those who had fallen were men of honour, received for answer that the atraktos—that is, the arrow—would be worth a great deal if it could tell men of honour from the rest; an allusion to the fact that the killed were those whom the stones and the arrows happened to hit.

On the arrival of the men, the Athenians decided to keep them in prison until the peace, and if the Peloponnesians invaded their country in the interval, to bring them out and put them to death. Meanwhile the defence of Pylos was not forgotten. The Messenians from Naupactus sent to their old country, to which Pylos had once belonged, some of the likeliest of their number, and began a series of incursions into Laconia, which their common dialect made all the more destructive. The Lacedaemonians, until then without experience of incursions or warfare of this kind, finding the Helots deserting and fearing the march of revolution in their country, began to grow seriously uneasy. Despite their unwillingness to betray this to the Athenians, they began to send envoys to Athens, and tried to recover Pylos and the prisoners. The Athenians, however, kept grasping at more, and dismissed envoy after envoy without their having achieved anything. Such was the history of the affair of Pylos.
